claim: Gene expression fundamentally shapes the structural and functional architecture of the human brain.
source: Gene expression fundamentally shapes the structural and functional architecture of the human brain.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established scientific consensus about the role of gene expression in brain organization.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas provides an unprecedented ability to examine gene expression mechanisms in vivo.
source: Open-access transcriptomic datasets like the Allen Human Brain Atlas provide an unprecedented ability to examine these mechanisms in vivo
evidence: This claim is supported by the existence and characteristics of the AHBA dataset as described in the manuscript.

claim: There is a lack of standardization across research groups in processing Allen Human Brain Atlas data.
source: however, a lack of standardization across research groups has given rise to myriad processing pipelines for using these data.
evidence: This is supported by the comprehensive review cited and the motivation for the current study.

claim: The abagen toolbox is an open-access software package for working with transcriptomic data.
source: Here, we develop the abagen toolbox, an open-access software package for working with transcriptomic data
evidence: This is a direct statement about the development of the software tool presented in the manuscript.

claim: Approximately 750,000 unique processing pipelines were applied to the Allen Human Brain Atlas data.
source: Applying three prototypical analyses to the outputs of 750,000 unique processing pipelines
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the scope of the analysis performed.

claim: Choice of pipeline has a large impact on research findings, with parameters influencing correlations by as much as ρ ≥ 1.0.
source: we find that choice of pipeline has a large impact on research findings, with parameters commonly varied in the literature influencing correlations between derived gene expression and other imaging phenotypes by as much as ρ ≥ 1.0.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis of the 750,000 pipelines.

claim: Processing steps that influence gene normalization yield the greatest impact on downstream statistical inferences.
source: Our results further reveal an ordering of parameter importance, with processing steps that influence gene normalization yielding the greatest impact on downstream statistical inferences and conclusions.
evidence: This is a key finding from the parameter importance analysis.

claim: Gene expression is a fundamental molecular phenotype that can be linked to biological pathway function.
source: Gene expression is particularly useful as it is a fundamental molecular phenotype that can be plausibly linked to the function of biological pathways (Whitaker et al., 2016; Seidlitz et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gene expression can be linked to protein synthesis.
source: Gene expression is particularly useful as it is a fundamental molecular phenotype that can be plausibly linked to the function of biological pathways (Whitaker et al., 2016; Seidlitz et al., 2018), protein synthesis (Zheng et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zheng et al., 2019.

claim: Gene expression can be linked to receptor distributions.
source: receptor distributions (Beliveau et al., 2017; Nørgaard et al., 2021; Shine et al., 2019; Deco et al., 2020; Preller et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Gene expression can be linked to cell types.
source: cell types (Hansen et al., 2021; Anderson et al., 2020b; Anderson et al., 2018; Seidlitz et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Acquiring high-quality transcriptomic data from the human brain is both costly and highly invasive.
source: Although there are numerous technical and analytic considerations, one foundational issue is that acquiring high-quality transcriptomic data from the human brain is both costly and highly invasive, requiring budgets far greater than most typical neuroimaging studies and restrictive access to tissue from post-mortem donors or cranial surgical patients.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical challenges of transcriptomic research based on general knowledge of the field.

claim: Multiple open-access repositories for gene expression in the human brain exist, including BrainSpan and PsychENCODE.
source: There exist multiple open-access repositories for gene expression in the human brain, including BrainSpan (Miller et al., 2014; Kang et al., 2011) and PsychENCODE (Gandal et al., 2018; Li et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018; among others: Sousa et al., 2017; Darmanis et al., 2015; Lake et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the respective datasets.

claim: BrainSpan and PsychENCODE datasets generally provide relatively sparse anatomical coverage.
source: however, these datasets generally provide relatively sparse anatomical coverage, limiting the types of analyses that can be performed.
evidence: This is a comparative statement about the characteristics of these datasets.

claim: Researchers comparing transcriptomic expression with whole-brain imaging-derived phenotypes have primarily relied on the Allen Human Brain Atlas.
source: Thus, researchers who aim to compare transcriptomic expression with whole-brain imaging-derived phenotypes have primarily relied on the Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA; Hawrylycz et al., 2012; Hawrylycz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reflects the research practice in the field.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas was initially released in 2010.
source: Initially released in 2010, the AHBA remains the most spatially comprehensive dataset of its kind.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the release date of the AHBA.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas is derived from bulk microarray analysis of tissue samples obtained from six donors.
source: Derived from bulk microarray analysis of tissue samples obtained from six donors, the AHBA provides expression data for more than 20,000 genes across 3702 brain areas in MRI-derived stereotactic space.
evidence: This is a factual description of the AHBA dataset.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas provides expression data for more than 20,000 genes across 3702 brain areas.
source: the AHBA provides expression data for more than 20,000 genes across 3702 brain areas in MRI-derived stereotactic space.
evidence: This is a factual description of the AHBA dataset content.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas has enabled dozens of studies examining relationships between gene expression and cortical thickness.
source: With its superior resolution, the AHBA has significantly contributed to the emergence of the field of imaging transcriptomics (Fornito et al., 2019), enabling dozens of studies over the past decade examining relationships between gene expression and an array of macroscale imaging attributes, including cortical thickness (Shin et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shin et al., 2018.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas has enabled studies examining relationships between gene expression and myelination.
source: myelination (Burt et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Burt et al., 2018.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas has enabled studies examining relationships between gene expression and developmental brain maturation.
source: developmental brain maturation (Whitaker et al., 2016; Kirsch and Chechik, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas has enabled studies examining relationships between gene expression and structural brain networks.
source: structural brain networks (Seidlitz et al., 2018; Romero-Garcia et al., 2018; Arnatkevičiūtė et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas has enabled studies examining relationships between gene expression and functional brain networks.
source: functional brain networks (Richiardi et al., 2015; Krienen et al., 2016; Vértes et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas has enabled studies examining relationships between gene expression and human cognition.
source: human cognition (Fox et al., 2014; Hansen et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The Allen Human Brain Atlas has highlighted the importance of whole-brain gene expression in neurological and psychiatric diseases.
source: The AHBA has also highlighted the importance of whole-brain gene expression in neurological and psychiatric diseases, where it has become increasingly clear that transcriptional pathways play a critical role in shaping the broader dynamics of disease progression and emergent symptomatology (Zheng et al., 2019; Shafiei et al., 2021; Henderson et al., 2019; Vogel et al., 2020; Rittman et al., 2016; Anderson et al., 2020a; Romme et al., 2017; McColgan et al., 2018; Morgan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Several software toolboxes have been developed to help researchers use transcriptional data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas.
source: Since its release, several software toolboxes have been developed to help researchers use transcriptional data from the AHBA (French and Paus, 2015; Gorgolewski et al., 2015; Rittman et al., 2017; Rizzo et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing toolboxes.

claim: Existing AHBA toolboxes often focus primarily on facilitating integration with neuroimaging data and offer limited functionality for modifying data processing.
source: however, these tools often focus primarily on facilitating integration of the AHBA with neuroimaging data, offering limited if any functionality for modifying how the data are processed prior to analysis.
evidence: This is an assessment of existing tools based on their documented capabilities.

claim: A comprehensive review revealed that many research groups have developed their own processing pipelines for the Allen Human Brain Atlas.
source: Instead, a recent comprehensive review revealed that many research groups have opted to develop their own processing pipelines for the AHBA (Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019.

claim: There are no field-accepted standards for processing imaging transcriptomic data.
source: Unfortunately, as there are no field-accepted standards for processing imaging transcriptomic data, the generated pipelines vary substantially across groups.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Methodological variability can have broad influences on analyses using structural MRI.
source: Indeed, over the past decade neuroimaging research has shown that methodological variability can have broad influences on analyses using structural MRI (Bhagwat et al., 2021; Kharabian Masouleh et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Methodological variability can have broad influences on analyses using diffusion MRI.
source: diffusion MRI (Oldham et al., 2020; Maier-Hein et al., 2017; Schilling et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Methodological variability can have broad influences on analyses using task fMRI.
source: task fMRI (Carp, 2012; Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Methodological variability can have broad influences on analyses using resting-state fMRI.
source: resting-state fMRI (Parkes et al., 2018; Ciric et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The lack of baseline gene expression datasets impedes the development of standardized practices.
source: Although researchers are beginning to grapple with the consequences of this variability, the lack of baseline gene expression datasets against which to compare new results impedes the development of standardized practices.
evidence: This is an inference about the challenges facing the field.

claim: Multiverse analyses involve analyzing all possible permutations of data processing and reporting the full range of analytic results.
source: In these situations, some researchers have proposed performing 'multiverse' analyses (Steegen et al., 2016; Dragicevic et al., 2019), wherein all possible permutations of data processing are analyzed and the full range of analytic results reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations defining multiverse analyses.

claim: Multiverse analyses can be computationally intensive.
source: Although such analyses can be computationally intensive, they offer a path to understand how processing choices impact statistical inferences and conclusions
evidence: This is a statement about the computational requirements of multiverse analyses.

claim: Multiverse analyses offer a path to understand how processing choices impact statistical inferences.
source: Although such analyses can be computationally intensive, they offer a path to understand how processing choices impact statistical inferences and conclusions, and provide a mechanism by which to help researchers converge on an optimal pipeline.
evidence: This is a statement about the benefits of multiverse analyses.

claim: The abagen toolbox collates all possible processing parameters into a set of turn-key workflows.
source: First, we develop an open-source Python toolbox, abagen, that collates all possible processing parameters into a set of turn-key workflows, optimized for flexibility and ease-of-use.
evidence: This is a description of the abagen toolbox functionality.

claim: The abagen toolbox was used to process the Allen Human Brain Atlas through approximately 750,000 unique pipelines.
source: We then use the toolbox to process the AHBA through approximately 750,000 unique pipelines.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the scope of the analysis.

claim: Three prototypical imaging transcriptomic analyses were performed to examine how different processing options modify derived statistical estimates.
source: Across three prototypical imaging transcriptomic analyses, we examine whether and how these different processing options modify derived statistical estimates and quantify the relative importance of each option.
evidence: This is a description of the analytical approach.

claim: A curated set of processing pipelines from the literature was replicated to assess how previously reported findings compare to the full range of potential outcomes.
source: Next, we replicate a curated set of processing pipelines from the literature to assess how previously reported findings compare to the full range of potential outcomes observed across all examined pipelines.
evidence: This is a description of the replication analysis performed.

claim: The abagen toolbox is available at https://github.com/rmarkello/abagen.
source: We introduce the abagen toolbox, an open-access software package designed to streamline processing and preparation of the AHBA for integration with neuroimaging data (Markello et al., 2021c, available at https://github.com/rmarkello/abagen; Markello, 2021b copy archived at swh:1:rev:2aeab5bd0f147fa76b488645e148a1c18095378d).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of the software.

claim: The abagen toolbox supports several workflows and offers functionality for an array of analyses.
source: Supporting several workflows, abagen offers functionality for an array of analyses and has already been used in several peer-reviewed publications and preprints (Shafiei et al., 2020; Hansen et al., 2021; Shafiei et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2021; Park et al., 2021; Valk et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2020; Benkarim et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2021; Park et al., 2020; Lariviere et al., 2020; Martins et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to publications using the toolbox.

claim: The primary abagen workflow integrates 17 distinct processing steps that have been employed in the published literature.
source: The primary workflow, used to generate regional gene expression matrices, integrates 17 distinct processing steps that have previously been employed by research groups throughout the published literature (Table 1).
evidence: This is a description of the workflow design based on literature review.

claim: Each unique set of processing choices and parameters is referred to as a 'pipeline'.
source: We refer to each unique set of processing choices and parameters as a 'pipeline'.
evidence: This is a definitional statement.

claim: 746,496 distinct processing pipelines were implemented.
source: From these 17 steps we implemented 746,496 distinct processing pipelines, where each pipeline parcellated microarray expression from the AHBA with the Desikan-Killiany atlas (Desikan et al., 2006) to generate a unique brain region-by-gene expression matrix.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the number of pipelines tested.

claim: Analyses of expression data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas can be grouped into three broad classes: correlated gene expression analyses, gene co-expression analyses, and regional gene expression analyses.
source: Analyses of expression data from the AHBA can be grouped into one of three broad classes (Fornito et al., 2019): correlated gene expression analyses, gene co-expression analyses, and regional gene expression analyses.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fornito et al., 2019.

claim: Correlated gene expression analyses examine the correlation between brain regions across genes, yielding a symmetric region × region matrix.
source: Correlated gene expression analyses examine the correlation between brain regions across genes, yielding a symmetric region × region matrix (similar to a functional connectivity matrix).
evidence: This is a definitional statement about a type of analysis.

claim: Gene co-expression analyses examine the correlation between genes across brain regions, yielding a symmetric gene × gene matrix.
source: Gene co-expression analyses, on the other hand, examine the correlation between genes across brain regions, yielding a symmetric gene × gene matrix.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about a type of analysis.

claim: Regional gene expression analyses examine the expression patterns of specific genes or gene sets in relation to other imaging-derived phenotypes.
source: Finally, regional gene expression analyses examine the expression patterns of specific genes or gene sets in relation to other imaging-derived phenotypes.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about a type of analysis.

claim: Previous work in other species has reliably observed that transcriptional similarity in the brain decays with increasing separation distance.
source: Previous work in other species has reliably observed that transcriptional similarity in the brain decays with increasing separation distance (Fulcher et al., 2019; Lau et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Distance-dependent relationship of transcriptional similarity is consistent with other imaging-derived phenotypes in humans.
source: This distance-dependent relationship is an expected feature due to the functional specialization of brain regions, and is consistent with other imaging-derived phenotypes in humans (Roberts et al., 2016; Goulas et al., 2019; Betzel and Bassett, 2018; Mišić et al., 2014; Shafiei et al., 2020; Horvát et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Spearman correlation between correlated gene expression and regional distance was computed for each pipeline.
source: We assessed this relationship by extracting the upper triangle of the correlated gene expression matrices and correlating them with the upper triangle of a regional distance matrix, derived by computing the average Euclidean distance between brain region centroids in the Desikan-Killiany atlas (Figure 1a, left panel).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the analysis performed.

claim: The relationship between correlated gene expression and distance is exponential.
source: Although previous work has highlighted that this relationship is exponential (Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019), we computed the Spearman correlation as both statistics should exhibit similar variability across pipelines and the latter is less computationally expensive.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Arnatkeviciute et al., 2019.

claim: Genes tend to form functional communities, exhibiting synchronized expression patterns across space and time.
source: A significant body of research has shown that genes tend to form functional communities, exhibiting synchronized expression patterns across space and time (Oldham et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Oldham et al., 2008.

claim: Gene co-expression patterns tend to be more similar within than between functional communities.
source: such that gene co-expression patterns tend to be more similar within than between such communities.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of gene communities.

claim: A silhouette score was calculated for gene co-expression matrices to measure how well gene communities represented the derived co-expression patterns.
source: We used these community assignments to calculate a silhouette score (Rousseeuw, 1987) for the gene co-expression matrices generated by each pipeline, measuring how well these communities represented the derived co-expression patterns (Figure 1a, middle panel).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the analysis performed.

claim: The T1w/T2w ratio is a robust phenotype that exhibits patterns of regional variation consistent with other microstructural and functional properties.
source: Recent work has highlighted that the T1w/T2w ratio is a robust phenotype that exhibits patterns of regional variation consistent with other microstructural and functional properties (Gao et al., 2020; Burt et al., 2018; Demirtaş et al., 2019; Fulcher et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The first principal component of gene expression was correlated with the whole-brain T1w/T2w ratio.
source: We therefore correlated the first principal component of gene expression with the whole-brain T1w/T2w ratio (Figure 1a, right panel), measuring the extent to which these values covary across the cortex.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the analysis performed.

claim: Choice of processing pipeline dramatically influences derived statistical estimates.
source: Results from these three analyses reveal that choice of processing pipeline dramatically influences derived statistical estimates (i.e. the CGE-distance correlation, the gene co-expression silhouette score, and the spatial correlations between gene PC1 and whole-brain T1w/T2w ratio; Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the analysis, supported by Figure 1b.

claim: The distribution of correlated gene expression estimates across pipelines ranges from -0.51 to -0.13.
source: We observe that all three of the generated distributions of statistical estimates across the 746,496 pipelines have wide ranges (correlated gene expression: [-0.51,–0.13]; gene co-expression: [-0.78,–0.18]; regional gene expression: [0.00, 0.90])
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The distribution of gene co-expression silhouette scores across pipelines ranges from -0.78 to -0.18.
source: gene co-expression: [-0.78,–0.18]
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The distribution of regional gene expression correlations across pipelines ranges from 0.00 to 0.90.
source: regional gene expression: [0.00, 0.90]
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the analysis.

claim: The distributions of statistical estimates are either bimodal or heavily skewed.
source: and are either bimodal (Figure 1b, left/middle panels) or heavily skewed (Figure 1b, right panel).
evidence: This is a descriptive finding about the distribution shapes, supported by Figure 1b.

claim: All pipelines demonstrate relatively poor fit of gene communities to the derived gene co-expression matrices.
source: While all the pipelines demonstrate relatively poor fit of gene communities to the derived gene co-expression matrices (refer to Materials and methods: Analytic approaches for information on why this is not unexpected)
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis with explanation provided in methods.

claim: A portion of the pipelines yield far worse correspondence of gene communities to gene co-expression matrices.
source: we observe that a portion of the pipelines yield far worse correspondence (Figure 1a and b, middle panels).
evidence: This is an observation from the analysis, supported by Figure 1.

claim: The parameter choices for pipelines yielding deviant results are not pathological and their use could be justified.
source: Notably, the parameter choices for these pipelines are not pathological—that is, their use could be justified—and, as we discuss later (see Results: Variability in parameter importance), modifying just one parameter setting can yield changes in effect sizes within this range.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the reasonableness of the pipeline choices.

claim: For all three analyses, there is substantial variability in the statistical estimates generated by different processing pipelines.
source: Collectively, we find that for all three of these analyses there is substantial variability in the statistical estimates generated by different processing pipelines, and this variability is large enough that, across pipelines, it has a meaningful difference in the potential inferences and conclusions that can be drawn.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analysis results.

claim: The variability in statistical estimates is large enough to have a meaningful difference in potential inferences and conclusions.
source: and this variability is large enough that, across pipelines, it has a meaningful difference in the potential inferences and conclusions that can be drawn.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion about the impact of the observed variability.

claim: Parameter importance was quantified by calculating a distribution of difference scores for each parameter.
source: We investigated parameter importance by calculating a distribution of difference scores for each parameter, measuring the extent to which changing each parameter—holding all other parameters constant—influences the derived statistical metrics from each of the three analyses.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the approach to quantifying parameter importance.

claim: There is considerable agreement in which parameters are the most impactful across analyses.
source: We find considerable agreement in which parameters are the most impactful across analyses (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter importance analysis, supported by Figure 2a.

claim: The most influential processing steps involve procedures that influence the gene normalization process.
source: the most influential processing steps often involve procedures that influence the gene normalization process in some way (e.g. gene normalization method, normalizing only matched samples; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter importance analysis, supported by Figure 2b.

claim: Among the least impactful parameters are choices concerning donor-specific probe selection and handling of missing data.
source: On the other hand, among the least impactful parameters are choices concerning donor-specific probe selection and handling of missing data.
evidence: This is a finding from the parameter importance analysis.

claim: Three of the six probe selection methods tested render the choice of donor-specific probe selection redundant.
source: It is worth noting that of the probe selection methods tested in the current manuscript (i.e. max intensity, correlation intensity, correlation variance, differential stability, RNAseq correlation, and averaging), three of the six all render the choice of donor-specific probe selection redundant.
evidence: This is an observation about the interaction between processing parameters.

claim: The Desikan-Killiany atlas is a relatively low-resolution atlas with 68 nodes.
source: We also highlight that choice of atlas may influence the impact of missing data handling: since the Desikan-Killiany atlas is a relatively low-resolution atlas (68 nodes), expression matrices generated from the tested pipelines are missing, at most, data for two brain regions.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the atlas used.

claim: Expression matrices generated from the tested pipelines are missing, at most, data for two brain regions.
source: expression matrices generated from the tested pipelines are missing, at most, data for two brain regions.
evidence: This is an observation about the data completeness in the analysis.

claim: Handling of missing data may be more important when higher-resolution parcellations are employed.
source: It is possible that handling of missing data may be more important when higher-resolution parcellations are employed.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about how results might differ with different atlases.

claim: Some parameters do not appear to affect results in aggregate but could play an important role for specific research questions.
source: That is, while some parameters do not appear to affect our results in aggregate, there are potentially specific research questions where these parameters could play an important and impactful role.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the context-dependence of parameter importance.

claim: The bimodality and skew observed in the full statistical distributions is almost entirely explained by the choice of gene normalization method.
source: Indeed, the bimodality and skew observed in the full statistical distributions for the analyses (Figure 1b) is almost entirely explained by this single parameter choice.
evidence: This is a finding about the dominant influence of gene normalization, supported by Figure 1b.

claim: The first two principal components explain 70% and 26% of variance, respectively.
source: We extracted the first two principal components from the statistical estimate matrix (variance explained: PC1 = 70%, PC2 = 26%)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the PCA analysis.

claim: The choice of gene normalization method distinguishes one-third of pipelines with no normalization from the remaining two-thirds that applied some form of normalization.
source: Reinforcing results presented above, we find that the choice of gene normalization method distinguishes the one-third of pipelines with no normalization (purple) from the remaining two-thirds that applied some form of normalization (blue and brown; Figure 2c, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis, supported by Figure 2c.

claim: Whether gene normalization was performed separately on samples within each structural class further delineates the pipelines that applied gene normalization into two distinct clusters.
source: For example, plotting the pipelines by whether the gene normalization was performed separately on samples within each structural class (i.e. cerebral cortex, subcortex, cerebellum) rather than across all tissue samples further delineates the pipelines that applied gene normalization into two distinct clusters (Figure 2c, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the PCA analysis, supported by Figure 2c.

claim: Parameters modifying normalization are the most important, followed by parameters influencing how tissue samples are matched to brain regions, and finally parameters impacting probe selection.
source: Broadly, parameters modifying normalization are the most important, followed by parameters influencing how tissue samples are matched to brain regions, and finally parameters impacting probe selection.
evidence: This is a summary finding about the hierarchy of parameter importance.

claim: Choices within each processing step do not all have an equivalent impact on derived estimates.
source: Moreover, we find that choices within each processing step do not all have an equivalent impact on derived estimates (i.e. performing no gene normalization has a much greater influence than choosing between the two other forms of normalization tested).
evidence: This is a finding about the differential impact of specific parameter choices.

claim: Nine peer-reviewed articles were selected that are highly-cited, highlight a wide range of processing options, and sufficiently describe their processing pipelines.
source: To investigate whether the subset of pipelines that have already been implemented in the published literature display similar variability, we used abagen to reproduce the processing procedures from nine peer-reviewed articles that (1) are highly-cited within the field, (2) highlight a wide range of processing options, and (3) sufficiently describe their processing pipelines such that they could be reproduced.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the selection criteria for the replication analysis.

claim: The Desikan-Killiany atlas was used for all reproduced pipelines to ensure comparability.
source: To ensure comparability, we standardized the choice of brain parcellation across pipelines, using the Desikan-Killiany atlas in all instances.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about standardization in the replication analysis.

claim: There are important differences in processing parameter selection among the reproduced pipelines.
source: In reproducing the pipelines we note important differences in processing parameter selection (Figure 3a)
evidence: This is an observation from the replication analysis, supported by Figure 3a.

claim: Variability in processing parameter selection results in slight discrepancies between gene expression values generated by the pipelines.
source: and find that this variability results in slight discrepancies between gene expression values generated by the pipelines.
evidence: This is a finding from the replication analysis.

claim: There is some variation in the distribution of cortical somatostatin (SST) between reproduced pipelines.
source: For example, looking at the distribution of cortical somatostatin (SST), a gene discussed heavily in Anderson et al., 2020b where it used as a proxy for somatostatin interneuron density (Fulcher, 2019), we observe some variation between pipelines (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is an observation from the replication analysis, supported by Figure 3b and c.

claim: There is moderate consistency in the statistical estimates generated by the reproduced pipelines.
source: Although we find moderate consistency in the statistical estimates generated by the pipelines, there are important differences (ranges: correlated gene expression [-0.49,–0.28], gene co-expression [-0.70,–0.24], regional gene expression [0.34, 0.88]; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a finding from the replication analysis, supported by Figure 3c.

claim: The range of correlated gene expression estimates from reproduced pipelines is -0.49 to -0.28.
source: correlated gene expression [-0.49,–0.28]
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the replication analysis.

claim: The range of gene co-expression estimates from reproduced pipelines is -0.70 to -0.24.
source: gene co-expression [-0.70,–0.24]
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the replication analysis.

claim: The range of regional gene expression estimates from reproduced pipelines is 0.34 to 0.88.
source: regional gene expression [0.34, 0.88]
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the replication analysis.

claim: One outlier pipeline did not appear to implement any form of gene normalization.
source: One outlier is the single pipeline that did not appear to implement any form of gene normalization (French and Paus, 2015), supporting earlier results demonstrating the importance of this processing step on downstream expression estimates.
evidence: This is an observation from the replication analysis with citation to the source.

claim: The processed expression data from the French and Paus 2015 pipeline were made openly available and have been used in analyses by other researchers.
source: This is potentially notable as the processed expression data from this pipeline were made openly available and have been used in analyses by other researchers (e.g. Sepulcre et al., 2018; Beliveau et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the reuse of data from one of the reproduced pipelines, supported by citations.

claim: Variation in processing can lead to similar inferences in specific analyses.
source: Although variation in processing can ostensibly lead to similar inferences in specific analyses, even minor differences in processing choices consistently yield measurable discrepancies in derived expression data.
evidence: This is an interpretive statement about the implications of the replication analysis.

claim: Even minor differences in processing choices consistently yield measurable discrepancies in derived expression data.
source: even minor differences in processing choices consistently yield measurable discrepancies in derived expression data.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the replication analysis.

claim: Without proper standardization, differences in processing will compound and become more problematic as the field continues to grow.
source: Without proper standardization, these differences will compound and become more problematic as the field continues to grow.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future implications.

claim: The abagen toolbox supports a workflow that accepts an atlas and returns a parcellated, preprocessed regional gene expression matrix.
source: The abagen toolbox supports two use-case driven workflows: (1) a workflow that accepts an atlas and returns a parcellated, preprocessed regional gene expression matrix (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is a description of toolbox functionality, supported by Figure 4a.

claim: The abagen toolbox supports a workflow that accepts a mask and returns preprocessed expression data for all tissue samples within the mask.
source: and, (2) a workflow that accepts a mask and returns preprocessed expression data for all tissue samples within the mask (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a description of toolbox functionality, supported by Figure 4b.

claim: Abagen workflows can be called via a single line of code from either the command line or Python terminal.
source: Workflows can be called via a single line of code from either the command line or Python terminal, and take approximately one minute to run with default settings using the Desikan-Killiany atlas.
